name: Ecamsule
lead: Ecamsule, sold under the trade name Mexoryl SX and known by the INCI name terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid, is a photostable organic UVA filter developed and patented by L'Oreal in 1982.[1][2] It absorbs ultraviolet light between roughly 290 and 400 nm, with a peak near 345 nm, and is typically combined with other filters (such as avobenzone and octocrylene) because it does not cover the whole UV range on its own.[2]

Sunscreens containing it have been sold in Europe, Canada and elsewhere since 1993. In the United States the FDA approved it in 2006 only within sunscreens registered under a New Drug Application, rather than as a general over-the-counter monograph ingredient.[2]

Published human studies on ecamsule-containing sunscreens report protection against UV-induced skin changes, and a 2019 trial measured absorption into the bloodstream under maximal-use conditions. No trial has examined it as a standalone appearance treatment.

paras: Ecamsule is used in daily-wear and sport sunscreens and in some moisturisers to absorb UVA, the part of the spectrum associated with photoaging and pigmentation. Because it is an acid, manufacturers usually neutralise it, commonly with triethanolamine, so it does not shift the product's pH.[2]
A registered trial examined UV and UV-visible light photoprotection in melasma, which concerns sunscreens as a category.[3]
Ecamsule absorbs UV photons and releases the energy as heat through reversible photoisomerisation. Wikipedia describes it as photostable, unlike avobenzone, which commonly needs a stabiliser.[2]

In a 2019 JAMA randomised trial, healthy volunteers applied four commercial sunscreens (containing avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene or ecamsule) under maximal-use conditions. Plasma concentrations of all the active ingredients, ecamsule included, exceeded the 0.5 ng/mL level at which FDA guidance calls for further nonclinical toxicology assessment. The authors noted this does not by itself indicate the ingredients are unsafe.[4]
A separate registered Phase 1 study (n=72) also assessed systemic absorption of sunscreen ingredients.[5] Wikipedia describes percutaneous absorption and systemic effects as low.[2]
A review of clinical studies of sunscreens containing Mexoryl SX concluded that they prevented several detrimental cutaneous effects of UV exposure.[6]

In human epidermis, a sunscreen containing terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid was compared with one containing octyl methoxycinnamate; both reduced dipyrimidine photolesions to a degree comparable to their protection against sunburn.[7] The persistent pigment darkening method has been used to evaluate in vivo UVA protection by filters including ecamsule.[8]
A 2025 review argued that newer filters such as ecamsule could improve public health if US sunscreen regulations were modernised.[9]

Wikipedia reports a mouse study found no increase in skin cancer promotion and that in vitro tests found no photomutagenicity.[2] An in vitro study in human keratinocytes and fibroblasts reported contradictory effects of various chemical filters under UV-induced oxidative stress.[10] Grokipedia states that the compound can cause serious eye irritation.[1]
A multi-centre European photopatch study (n=1000) is registered to examine photocontact dermatitis to sunscreen allergens.[11]

Per Grokipedia, ecamsule is permitted in the EU at up to 10% (as acid), in Canada since 1994, in Australia since 1995, and in Japan at up to 3%.[1] In the US, Wikipedia notes there is no official UVA rating system and that approval applies to NDA-registered sunscreens.[2]

Human studies of ecamsule have been conducted on sunscreen products rather than on the ingredient as an appearance treatment. They include the 2019 absorption trial,[4] a pigment-darkening UVA assessment,[8] an epidermal DNA-photolesion study,[7] a review of clinical results,[6] and registered trials on melasma photoprotection[3] and systemic absorption.[5]

timeline.event: Sunscreens containing it go on sale in Europe and Canada.[2]
US FDA approves it within NDA-registered sunscreens.[2]
JAMA trial measures plasma levels of four sunscreen actives, including ecamsule.[4]

card.summary: L'Oreal's photostable UVA filter, Mexoryl SX; established in sunscreens abroad, US-approved only via NDA products.
card.aka: Mexoryl SX, terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid
card.note: Systemic absorption above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold was measured in a 2019 trial.

quick.overview:
Ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) is a UVA-absorbing sunscreen ingredient developed by L'Oreal in the 1980s. It is valued for photostability and is usually paired with other filters.

It has been sold in Europe and Canada since the 1990s; in the US it is approved only in sunscreens registered through a New Drug Application.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVA light and dissipates the energy as heat, remaining chemically stable under sunlight.
quick.risks: A 2019 JAMA trial found sunscreen actives including ecamsule were absorbed into plasma above the FDA's screening threshold; the authors did not conclude this meant harm. Other sources describe low systemic effects and no photomutagenicity in vitro.
